kobeissi-margin-debt-net-credit-record:
A fresh sign of investors piling into stocks with borrowed money rather than cash has emerged. According to The Kobeissi Letter, net credit balances (the cash investors hold in brokerage accounts minus margin debt) fell $70 billion in June to a record negative $1.06 trillion. Margin debt itself climbed $895 billion over the same period to a record $1.50 trillion.

## Checking the numbers first
FINRA's own raw data confirms these figures almost exactly. June 2026 margin debt came to $1.502 trillion, and combined free credit balances across cash and margin accounts came to $440.9 billion. Subtract one from the other and you get negative $1.061 trillion, matching Kobeissi's figure closely.

@@REF@@This $1.5 Trillion Bomb Is Waiting to Blow Up Your Portfolio (Yahoo Finance/24/7 Wall St, 2026-07-25)|https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/1-5-trillion-bomb-waiting-131609949.html|https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/C6546FDF461C878C9BA01744731492C8CEA7B22A2941C3684FB9EB482F3D11CA/subgraphmysterio/resizefill_w1200_h624;quality_80;format_webp/https:%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2F24_7_wall_st__718%2F87e712288d9edb5fbba769de6657ff28

## But 'broad risk appetite' may only be half the story
Kobeissi contrasts this with 2008, when investors held more cash and net credit balances were positive. Other sources, though, put both the 2000 dot-com peak (-$130 billion) and the 2008 peak (-$60 billion) in negative territory, suggesting this comparison may be mixing different measurement methodologies. That discrepancy isn't fully resolved as of this writing.

The stronger evidence is about where the leverage is actually concentrated. Per Crypto Briefing, leveraged ETFs hold about $179 billion in total assets, and 85% of that sits in just three sectors: tech, AI and semiconductors. On June 5, a 3x leveraged semiconductor ETF fell 31% in a single session. In July, South Korea's Kospi dropped 27% after SK hynix said it would slow AI memory expansion, triggering margin calls across roughly 1.2 million Korean brokerage accounts, about 10% of all trading accounts in the country, that had bet on the sector through leveraged ETFs.

@@REF@@Korea's AI Stock Rout Is Becoming a Lesson in Leveraged Excess (Bloomberg, 2026-07-14)|https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-14/korea-s-ai-stock-rout-is-becoming-a-lesson-in-leveraged-excess

@@CMP@@Kobeissi's read|Investor risk appetite is at unprecedented levels.|What other sources suggest|The leverage isn't spread broadly, it's concentrated in AI and semiconductor leveraged ETFs and derivatives, and that structure has already blown up once, in Korea.
"Investors love risk across the board" and "leverage is stacked in one AI-shaped corner of the market" paint very different pictures of what happens in the next pullback.

## Has margin debt historically warned of corrections
Three prior episodes of margin debt surging more than 65%, March 2000 (dot-com), July 2007 (financial crisis) and October 2021 (2022 bear market), all preceded market tops by roughly two to six months. This is being counted as a fourth instance of the pattern. The sample size is only three or four cycles, though, and some analysts note debt and markets tend to rise together, making this more of a coincident indicator than a precise timing tool.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: is a record-low net credit balance a warning for the whole market, or a risk concentrated in one AI/semiconductor-shaped corner of it.

If cracks show up first in sector-specific leveraged products, as they did in Korea, it's the latter. If a pullback spreads across the broader market, the former reading was right. Margin debt doesn't cause a decline, but once one starts, it can make it bigger.
jukan-korea-memory-mega-mou-950b:
SK hynix agreed to supply $750 billion (about 1,085 trillion won) worth of advanced memory chips to Nvidia and other US tech giants over the next five years. The same day, Samsung Electronics signed a separate memorandum of understanding with Broadcom covering $200 billion (about 290 trillion won) in memory supply and foundry cooperation, also over five years. Both were announced by Kim Yong-beom, South Korea's presidential chief of staff for policy, during President Lee Jae-myung's Silicon Valley trip, relayed by chip-industry commentator Jukan on X.

## Samsung's $200 billion with Broadcom checks out
Samsung's own newsroom release confirms this almost word for word: "more than $200 billion across memory and foundry" over five years. Fortune independently confirmed the same figure through its own reporting.

@@REF@@Samsung Electronics and Broadcom Expand Strategic Collaboration Across Memory and Foundry Technologies (Samsung Newsroom, 2026-07-25)|https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-and-broadcom-expand-strategic-collaboration-across-memory-and-foundry-technologies|https://img.global.news.samsung.com/global/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/25142854/Samsung-Semiconductors-Memory-and-Foundry-Technologies-Broadcom-MoU_Thumb932_F.jpg

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said, the same day, in his own words: "SK Group and I are announcing today that our two companies will enter into business partnerships that will represent over $500 billion of business together." That $500 billion spans not just SK hynix's memory supply but SK Telecom's AI infrastructure, an investment in Naver, Hyundai robotics, LG, and an AI Frontier Lab, the whole SK Group conglomerate. The government's $750 billion figure appears to layer on additional pieces, including a separate SK hynix-Microsoft supply deal, under the broader "SK-Nvidia and others" framing. The two numbers are counting different things, so reading $750 billion as "the memory contract with Nvidia alone" overstates what's actually there.

@@REF@@Nvidia, SK to announce $500 billion partnership, Jensen Huang says (Korea Herald, 2026-07-25)|https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10819890|https://wimg.heraldcorp.com/news/cms/2026/07/25/news-p.v1.20260725.84bb149612514e73b1311fe2aa1af0c0_T1.jpg

SK hynix's own newsroom release calls this a "Letter of Intent," meaning a framework requiring further negotiation, not a binding contract. But policy chief Kim Yong-beom pushed back directly on that framing in a Seoul Economic Daily interview, saying "this isn't simply a corporate MOU, expect quite large, meaningful numbers from investment attraction, strategic alliances, and long-term contracts." The people announcing the deal and the people drafting it are describing it differently.

jukan-apple-micron-china-memory-lobbying:
Apple is lobbying the White House to allow Chinese-made memory chips in its products, according to the Wall Street Journal. The chips in question come from Chinese DRAM maker CXMT and NAND maker YMTC. Micron, the US memory chipmaker, is reportedly pushing back hard, arguing the move should never be allowed. Chip-industry commentator Jukan, writing on X, disputed Apple's reasoning.

## This is a blacklist fight, not a tariff fight
The dispute is about export-control and national-security blacklists, not tariff exemptions. Two separate lists are in play: the Pentagon's "1260H list," which designates CXMT as a Chinese military-linked company, and Commerce's Entity List, which would effectively cut off US companies from doing business with CXMT if it's added. Apple is lobbying to keep CXMT off that list, not asking for a tariff discount.

## 'CXMT is cheap' is only half true
A July 26 comparison by Tom's Hardware found CXMT's 64GB DDR5 module priced about 2.2% below equivalent Samsung/SK hynix modules, despite a 40% larger die and worse yields. WCCFTech reported the same finding from Computex in June: "CXMT cheap is a myth, prices are almost on par with the big three." Apple's real motive for wanting CXMT appears to be supply, not price. While Samsung, SK hynix and Micron divert capacity toward AI-driven HBM, CXMT has no reason to make that pivot, leaving it with relatively more available inventory and flexible contract terms.

@@REF@@Chinese CXMT DRAM doesn't look like the budget savior many were expecting (Tom's Hardware, 2026-07-26)|https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/dram/chinese-cxmt-dram-doesnt-look-like-the-budget-savior-many-were-expecting-new-modules-enter-the-market-but-prices-still-track-the-big-three|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/Y6RXNGdt5atPtqKHjD7EUW-1280-80.jpg

## The '$250 price hike' isn't a settled fact yet either
Jukan argued memory prices jumped roughly fivefold while raising Apple's per-unit cost by only $50, even as Apple raised iPhone prices by $250. Checking this, Apple hasn't actually raised iPhone prices yet. The real price increases announced June 25 hit Macs, iPads and Vision Pro: MacBook Air up $200, MacBook Pro up $500, Vision Pro up $500. The $250 figure is an IDC-style projection for the unreleased iPhone 18 Pro (estimates range $100-270, mostly clustered around $200), not a hike that's already happened. Separately, iPhone 17 prices did rise in Japan, but Forbes attributed that to a weak yen, not memory costs. The "$50 memory cost versus $250 iPhone hike" comparison mixes something that's already happened with something projected, and two different causes.

## The Micron-Apple grudge is real, though
One of Jukan's other claims holds up well. Reports sourced to the WSJ confirm Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra has a genuinely long-running tension with Apple, dating back to his time as a SanDisk co-founder in 1988, when he reportedly avoided meeting Apple representatives altogether. Mehrotra met directly with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last week to oppose Apple's request, offering Micron's $250 billion US manufacturing investment through 2035 (Idaho, New York, Virginia) as the alternative.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: is Apple's lobbying really about protecting consumers from price increases, or cover for securing supply.

If Apple wins approval for CXMT and YMTC and iPhone prices come down or hold steady, supply really was the goal. If prices go up anyway after approval, the "inflation protection" framing won't hold up.

meru-treasury-yield-deficit-not-just-oil:
The 10-year Treasury yield broke above 4.7% intraday. Meru argues oil alone can't explain this, pointing out that breakeven inflation has barely moved while the 30-year real yield jumped to its highest since the 2008 financial crisis.

## Did breakeven inflation really stay flat
Checking Meru's core premise first, an Axios report from July 23 backs it up directly: the bond market's long-run inflation pricing has barely changed even as Treasury yields have climbed. The 10-year breakeven rate stayed between 2.20% and 2.28% all month.
Meanwhile the 30-year real yield climbed to 2.95%, the highest since this metric started being tracked in 2010. Bloomberg reported on July 9 that a 30-year auction drew the highest yield since 2007. Meru's read, that this is about the cost of money itself rather than inflation, holds up against the data.

@@REF@@Higher Treasury yields signal new era for interest rates (Axios, 2026-07-23)|https://www.axios.com/2026/07/23/

## But is the IEEPA refund figure accurate
No. The card's claim of $180 billion a year through 2036 isn't accurate. The actual Penn Wharton Budget Model estimate from February 20, 2026 puts the refund liability from the IEEPA tariff ruling at $175-182 billion, a one-time total, not a recurring annual figure. CNBC and Reuters independently reported the same $175 billion refund number.
The through 2036 framing belongs to a different estimate. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget separately projected the ruling could cost $1.7-1.9 trillion in cumulative lost revenue through 2036, a $2.2-2.4 trillion debt impact with interest, which averages to roughly $150-190 billion a year. It looks like two different institutions' two different numbers got merged into one.

@@REF@@Supreme Court tariffs ruling could put U.S. on hook for $175 billion in refunds (CNBC, 2026-02-20)|https://www.cnbc.com/2026/02/20/

## What about the rest of the argument
China selling Treasuries while buying gold, Japanese investors net-selling $29.6 billion in Q1 2026, and record global corporate bond issuance of $3.68 trillion in H1 2026 with Amazon's $54 billion deal, all check out independently through Nikkei Asia, CNBC and other outlets.
One wrinkle: Amazon said after that bond sale it won't issue more debt in 2026 (CNBC, July 7), so whether Big Tech's bond rush keeps up the same pace is worth watching.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
If this is about oil, yields should fall once the Strait of Hormuz reopens, a matter of weeks. If it's about supply and demand, it only eases once the deficit and corporate bond issuance slow down, a matter of years.
One number needs correcting, but the core diagnosis, flat inflation expectations paired with rising real yields, holds up. The next thing to check is whether the Treasury's August 5 quarterly refunding announcement drops the language guaranteeing stable auction sizes, as Meru flagged.
serenity-aaoi-pluggables-cpo-coexist:
The debate over whether co-packaged optics (CPO) will soon make traditional pluggable optical transceivers obsolete in AI data centers got a reality check this week. Analyst Serenity relayed comments from a photonics-industry CEO, made on a podcast, arguing pluggables have roughly another decade of relevant commercial life left, not months.

## Who is this CEO, actually
It turns out the comment didn't come from an AAOI executive at all. It came from Vickram Vathulya, CEO of Sivers Semiconductors, a Swedish company that makes continuous-wave (CW) lasers. The podcast was Laser Focus World's "Expert Insights: Photonics & AI," aired July 21, with Oriole CEO James Regan also on the call. Sivers sells laser components into both CPO and pluggable supply chains, worth noting since it has little to lose either way this debate resolves.

The exchange started with a reader asking whether Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) is in trouble as CPO gains traction. Serenity's answer: not exactly. AAOI is also developing CPO technology, just further behind on commercializing it than some peers.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_%283706444821%29.jpg/960px-Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_%283706444821%29.jpg|A rack of GPUs in an AI data center. The optical cabling that links racks like this is what's actually being argued over.|ChrisDag · CC BY 2.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_(3706444821).jpg

## The claim mostly checks out anyway
Independent of Vathulya's framing, real industry data leans toward pushing back on the idea that CPO is about to take over. SemiAnalysis, in a June report, pushed full CPO mass production out to 2028-2029, citing yield math: a single optical engine might yield 95%, but with 32 engines per switch, system-level yield drops to around 19%.

@@REF@@Lumentum and the Laser Bottleneck (Chipstrat, 2026-03-02)|https://www.chipstrat.com/p/lumentum-and-the-laser-bottleneck|https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!owi8!,w_1200,h_675,c_fill,f_jpg,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep,g_auto/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd93bd343-8456-4a66-a2bf-7fc4c7ff155d_1200x630.jpeg

Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston has said the company is "undershipping our customers' demand by somewhere around 30%." Nvidia locked in $2 billion each with Lumentum and Coherent in March, $4 billion total, to secure priority laser supply.

@@REF@@AI Data Center Optical Component Shortage: Nvidia's $4B Laser Lockup Pushes Rivals Past 2027 (Tech Times, 2026-05-27)|https://www.techtimes.com/articles/317281/20260527/ai-data-center-optical-component-shortage-nvidias-4b-laser-lockup-pushes-rivals-past-2027.htm|https://d.techtimes.com/en/full/465511/diagram-hardware-components-within-nvidia-photonics-co-packaged.png

AAOI itself confirmed on its May earnings call that an industry-wide indium phosphide laser shortage is likely to persist, and said it plans to expand its own laser capacity by 350% by 2027.

## A third option: near-package optics
The CEO's bigger point, as relayed, is that the industry is heading toward several coexisting architectures rather than one clean winner. Besides pluggables and CPO, there's a newer category called near-package optics (NPO), which sits closer to the chip than a pluggable without going as far as full co-packaging. Component makers including Credo, Marvell, Coherent and Lumentum are confirmed to be building in this space. It's less clear whether Nvidia or Broadcom use the NPO label in their own switch roadmaps, which suggests NPO is more a component-supplier category riding alongside the CPO platforms than a named hyperscaler initiative.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: if pluggables, CPO and NPO all coexist for a decade, which optical suppliers actually win.

What holds back all three paths isn't which architecture wins, it's laser and raw-material supply. The longer CPO slips, the longer pluggables stay relevant, and the bigger NPO's window gets too. This is secondhand color from a podcast relayed through a tweet, but its direction lines up with what the industry data actually shows.
kobeissi-m2-outpaces-gdp-g7:
Money creation keeps outpacing real economic growth across the G7, according to The Kobeissi Letter. Its figures show Canada's M2 money supply up 368% since January 2004, the largest increase in the G7, while the Canadian economy grew just 159% in nominal terms over the same period.

## Checking it against independent data
A separate analysis citing Bank of Canada monetary aggregates puts Canada's M2 growth at roughly 362% from March 2004 to June 2026, close enough to Kobeissi's 368% to fall within a reasonable margin.

@@REF@@Canada Never Stopped Printing: M2 Money Supply Surges 362% Since 2004 (Invest Offshore, 2026-07-22)|https://investoffshore.com/canada-never-stopped-printing-m2-money-supply-surges-362-since-2004/|https://investoffshore.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Canada-and-G7-M2-Money-Supply-Growth.png

The St. Louis Fed's FRED data on the US M2-to-GDP ratio tells a consistent story: that ratio rose from roughly 50% in 2004 to 75-78% recently, backing Kobeissi's claim that US M2 (up 279%) has structurally outpaced nominal GDP (up 171%).

@@REF@@M2 to GDP Ratio (FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis)|https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/?g=eTtE|https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.png?width=880&height=440&g=eTtE

## Japan is the quiet opposite case
Japan, by contrast, saw M2 grow just 90% since 2004, but its economy grew only 25%, the slowest in the G7. That low-low combination lines up with Japan's well-documented "lost decades" of stagnant growth and low inflation.

@@CMP@@Money-outpacing-growth group (Canada, US, France, eurozone)|Money creation is fast, growth lags well behind, and the gap keeps widening|Stagnation group (Japan)|Both money creation and growth are weak, so the gap is small but neither is moving

## What this gap actually means
The exact decimal points don't all match across sources, but the direction holds up across independent data. In economies where money supply is growing far faster than output, that gap slowly dilutes currency value and builds long-run pressure on asset prices and inflation.
trump-xi-putin-no-weapons-iran:
President Trump wrote on Truth Social that Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin both personally promised him they will not sell weapons to Iran.
He said Xi's pledge extends to Chinese companies too, and that he is doing Xi "very big favors" in return.

## What state is the Iran war actually in
The war is real. It began February 28, 2026, and Trump's July 23 statement lands exactly on day 145.
The US and Israel are fighting Iran, with Hezbollah aligned to Tehran and the Houthis opening a second front by blockading Saudi shipping routes on July 20.
Two ceasefires, in April and June, each collapsed. Trump declared the June memorandum "over" at the NATO Ankara summit on July 8.
Iran did reject a US-backed ceasefire proposal put forward by Iraqi mediators.
But CNBC reported on July 27 that the war has since paused to give peace talks "space," an ambiguous state that is neither a clean ceasefire nor open war.

## Did China actually confirm anything
China's foreign ministry did not confirm the pledge itself.
Instead it reaffirmed Iran as a "comprehensive strategic partner" and backed Iran's sovereignty, security and dignity, a generic statement that neither confirms nor denies Trump's framing.

## What did Russia actually deny
Foreign Minister Lavrov, speaking after ASEAN talks in Manila, said Russia isn't supplying weapons to Iran and that Moscow wants de-escalation in the Strait of Hormuz.
That's a separate denial, not a direct confirmation of the personal pledge Trump described.
What matters more is a different US allegation: that Russia fed Iran targeting data and supplied upgraded Shahed drones.
The Kremlin denied only "military transactions" on that point, not the intelligence-sharing allegation itself.

@@REF@@Trump Says Putin Assured Him Russia Is Staying Out: American Officials Say Moscow Fed Iran Targeting Data (National Security Journal, 2026-07-24)|https://nationalsecurityjournal.org/trump-says-putin-assured-him-russia-is-staying-out-american-officials-say-moscow-fed-iran-targeting-data/|https://nationalsecurityjournal.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/B-1B-Lancer-Bomber-1.jpg

@@CMP@@Trump's account|Both Xi and Putin promised, and it would be "very bad for them" to break it.|What's actually confirmed|China never confirmed the pledge, and Russia denied only arms sales, not the separate intelligence-sharing allegation. The war itself is paused, not over.
Whether to take the statement at face value or discount the unconfirmed half comes down to that gap.

@@REF@@Trump says he trusts Putin, Xi that Russia, China are not supplying weapons to Iran (TASS, 2026-07-24)|https://tass.com/world/2165073|https://tass.com/img/blocks/common/tass_logo_share_eng.png

What the "very big favors" refers to is also unclear.
A May Beijing summit did produce a US-China trade deal covering tariff cuts, rare-earth exports and Chinese soybean purchases, but no reporting directly links that deal to the Iran arms question. That connection is Trump's own framing.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
Only one thing actually settles this: whether Chinese or Russian weapons show up in Iran regardless of what was said.
Trump's accounts of foreign leaders' promises have diverged from his own officials' descriptions before.
Whether this pledge holds will show up in the war's next phase, specifically whether the Hormuz blockade eases or tightens further.
jukan-amd-mi500-tam-14t:
Chip-industry commentator Jukan relayed a note from analyst Jeff Pu raising the AI accelerator market forecast to $1.4 trillion by 2030, up from $1 trillion, alongside claims that AMD's MI455X delivers 34 times the throughput and an 18th of the cost per token of its predecessor, already beating Nvidia's B200 on some workloads.

## Where does that number actually come from
According to Business Standard, the $1.4 trillion figure traces directly to AMD CEO Lisa Su's own keynote at AMD's Advancing AI event in San Jose on July 22.
She told the audience compute infrastructure spending would reach $2 trillion by 2030 (up from $365 billion in 2025), with the AI accelerator market itself growing to roughly $1.4 trillion.
Jeff Pu is a real analyst, a managing director at GF Securities in Hong Kong, but his background is Apple and hardware supply chains, not AI datacenter market modeling.
Gate News reported GF Securities raised its AMD price target to $640 around the same event, consistent with a note relaying the company's own guidance rather than independent bottoms-up research.

kobeissi-oracle-cds-record: Oracle's cost of insuring against a default has hit a record, with five-year credit default swaps trading near 203 basis points, meaning investors now pay roughly $203,000 a year to insure $10 million of the company's debt against non-payment, The Kobeissi Letter reports. That level has more than quadrupled since mid-2025 and now sits above where Oracle's CDS traded at the peak of the 2008 financial crisis. The stress shows up in the bond market too. Oracle's 6.7% notes due 2056 widened 8 basis points this week to a 263 basis point spread over Treasurys, and its 5.7% notes due 2036 widened 9 basis points to 205. S&P Global Ratings downgraded Oracle to BBB-, one notch above junk, on July 9th, citing the company's fast-growing spending on AI data centers. Oracle has taken on debt at an unusual pace to build out cloud capacity for AI customers including OpenAI, and investors are increasingly pricing in the risk that revenue from those contracts doesn't arrive fast enough to cover the bill. A further downgrade to junk status would raise Oracle's borrowing costs even more and could trigger selling by funds that only hold investment-grade debt.
jukan-samsung-hynix-silicon-valley-deal:
Ahead of President Lee Jae-myung's Silicon Valley trip, presidential chief of staff for policy Kim Yong-beom previewed 'very large-scale' supply contracts for Samsung Electronics and SK hynix with major US tech firms, without naming which companies or whether the deals covered memory, foundry work, or both.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_%283706444821%29.jpg/960px-Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_%283706444821%29.jpg|A cluster built from many GPUs stacked together, the kind of infrastructure these AI deals are meant to feed.|ChrisDag · CC BY 2.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_(3706444821).jpg

## The vague preview turned into hard numbers within days
On July 25, what actually got announced was far more specific than the preview. Samsung signed a roughly $200 billion, five-year deal (through 2030) with Broadcom covering HBM supply for AI accelerators, sub-2nm foundry production and advanced packaging.

@@REF@@Samsung wins $200 billion order to supply chips to Broadcom (Fortune, 2026-07-25)|https://fortune.com/2026/07/25/samsung-200-billion-order-supply-2-nanometer-chips-broadcom/|https://fortune.com/img-assets/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/GettyImages-2284413802-e1785010814998.jpg?resize=1200,600

## SK hynix's side involved both Nvidia and Microsoft
SK Group signed a roughly $500 billion letter of intent with Nvidia covering multi-gigawatt AI data-center buildout and long-term HBM supply, and separately reportedly extended HBM4 supply to Microsoft. SK's combined big-tech partnerships were put at roughly $750 billion over five years.

@@REF@@NVIDIA Secures SK Hynix HBM Memory In $500B AI Infrastructure Deal (HotHardware, 2026-07-25)|https://hothardware.com/news/nvidia-secures-sk-hynix-hbm-memory-500b-ai-infrastructure-deal|https://hothardware.com/contentimages/NewsItem/71209/content/16x9_2133x1200_highres-nvidia-sign.jpg

Worth flagging: the roughly $250 billion figure attributed to Microsoft is derived by subtracting Nvidia's $500 billion from SK's $750 billion total in one syndicated report, not a standalone confirmed number.

## The presidential office confirmed the total itself
At the San Francisco AI Summit, Kim Yong-beom said Korean firms and US big tech agreed to roughly $950 billion in semiconductor cooperation, pointing directly to the Samsung-Broadcom and SK hynix-Nvidia deals as the substance of his earlier preview. The Korea Herald report carrying those remarks describes the Samsung-Broadcom agreement as a $200 billion memorandum of understanding and folds SK's side into a single $750 billion figure covering Nvidia and other global tech firms, so the $500 billion Nvidia-only breakout above does not appear in that article.

@@REF@@Korea, US tech giants set sights on $950 billion in chip partnerships: Seoul (The Korea Herald, 2026-07-25)|https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10819973|https://wimg.heraldcorp.com/news/cms/2026/07/25/news-p.v1.20260725.a5b80da090f14900a17fe9e42ce7e871_T1.jpg

## What this preview actually left behind
It's unusual for commercial contracts normally negotiated privately between companies to land on numbers that match a presidential-level preview this closely. The thing to watch now is whether Samsung keeps expanding beyond Nvidia and Broadcom, and whether the Microsoft figure gets an independent confirmation of its own.

Whether Samsung lands a major customer beyond Nvidia will be settled by the actual signed deal, not by how vivid the buildup sounds.
jukan-chip-equipment-lead-times-double:

## The direction got reconfirmed five days later
DigiTimes reported on July 28 that Samsung and SK hynix are placing orders early to get ahead of lead times that could reach a full year, reconfirming the broader trend.

## But the specific figures sit in one article alone
The claim that the top five, Applied Materials, ASML, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron and KLA, control about 70% of the global market, and that Korean suppliers feeding TSMC and Micron saw lead times stretch from three-four months to six-eight months, both trace only to that single Electronic Times piece. The suppliers are anonymized as "Company A" and "Company B," so they can't be identified.

@@CMP@@Confirmed|The direction itself, lead times stretching (reported independently by two outlets)|Unconfirmed|The 70% share figure and the 3-4-month-to-6-8-month range (from one article only)

## Is there another explanation
Both articles frame this as demand overwhelming supply from simultaneous global fab investment, not as equipment makers prioritizing certain customers over others.

## So how should these numbers be treated
The direction, lead times lengthening, is credible since two outlets reported it independently. But numbers as specific as 70% or "three-four months to six-eight months" rest on a single source and should be read that way. Whether Samsung and SK hynix's new fabs actually open late will be the real test of this story.
kobeissi-iran-rejects-ceasefire:
The New York Times reported July 23, citing Iranian and Iraqi officials, that Iran rejected a ceasefire proposal Iraq conveyed on the United States' behalf. Iraqi Prime Minister al-Zaidi reportedly carried the proposal to Tehran after meeting President Trump at the White House, and Iran dismissed it as a "temporary deal" that dodged the Strait of Hormuz question.

## Iraq denied the whole thing within a day
Iraq's prime minister's office and the Iraqi News Agency officially rebutted the report on July 24, calling it "completely baseless" and disconnected from reality. Al-Zaidi's own office separately said his Tehran visit was only meant to encourage "peace and dialogue," a materially softer description than actually brokering a US ceasefire proposal.

## The "145th day" count is also off
The Kobeissi Letter marked this as day 145 of the war, but counting from the war's February 28 start, July 24 is actually day 147. Two days may seem small, but when markets frame war risk around exactly how many days it's run, getting the count right is its own detail worth getting straight.

## So what's actually confirmed here
Only two things hold up: Iran rejected some US-linked proposal (per Iranian officials), and Iraq denies it was ever the broker of that proposal. At least one part of "Iraq brokered it, Iran rejected it" conflicts with the parties' own denial, and the day count needs correcting too when weighing how this feeds into war-risk pricing.
jukan-cxmt-huawei-premium:
Changxin Memory Technologies (CXMT), the Chinese state-linked memory chipmaker, has grown powerful enough to push back even on partners as large as Huawei, semiconductor analyst Jukan reports, citing Reuters.

## Charging more than the industry's old price-setter
Reuters reports that CXMT has been charging more than Samsung Electronics's roughly $1,240 per unit for comparable 64GB DDR5 server memory modules in recent weeks, a figure sourced to people familiar with the matter rather than a public price list.

## A pricing standoff pulled engineers out of the fab
When CXMT pushed for a price increase, engineers from SiCarrier, a Huawei-linked equipment and maintenance vendor working inside CXMT's Hefei facility, were reportedly told to leave in June after tension over the demand. Some coverage frames this loosely as CXMT versus Huawei directly, but the engineers involved worked for SiCarrier, not Huawei itself.

@@REF@@CXMT Reportedly Outprices Samsung for DDR5 Server Memory Amid Surging Demand (TechPowerUp, 2026-07-24)|https://www.techpowerup.com/351063/cxmt-reportedly-outprices-samsung-for-ddr5-server-memory-amid-surging-demand|https://www.techpowerup.com/img/kGQxBA02JNNQy6AD.jpg

## The US market is the goal, but capacity isn't there yet
Three sources tell Reuters that CXMT wants to eventually sell into the US market too, though for now its production is stretched just meeting Chinese demand. New fabs in Hefei and Shanghai could more than double its capacity to over 600,000 wafers a month by 2027, which is when a US push would become more realistic.

CXMT makes DRAM, the everyday memory chip used in phones, PCs, and servers, and has been one of the forces squeezing global memory supply this year, a dynamic that has helped lift prices for Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron alike.

## Is this one supplier's moment, or a real shift in leverage
That CXMT can now out-price Samsung and make a Huawei-linked vendor's engineers leave over a pricing dispute suggests the balance of power in memory chips may be moving faster than the industry's shared story, that scarcity lifts everyone's margins together, would suggest.
